projects.title: The Stolen Archive
projects.description: A virtual museum of 30 looted colonial objects that shows how each one left home, who claims it and who holds it today.
projects.introText: The Stolen Archive is a virtual exhibition of thirty objects taken during colonial wars, conquests and excavations, from the Benin Bronzes to the Parthenon Marbles. It works as a companion to a museum visit and as a museum of its own, and asks who was able to take these objects, who keeps them and who has managed to get them back.

gridImages.caption: Five eras of appropriation, from the spoils of Europe's wars to world wars and returns.
Three ways through the archive: choose a tour, then how long and how complex the texts should be.
The collection: thirty objects from five continents, filterable by region.
Object page for the Benin Bronzes, with where they were made, where they are held and how they left.
Whose object is it? The claimant's and the holder's positions side by side, each with its sources.
The Timeline tour, one of three readings of the same thirty objects.

projects.middleText: Visitors pick one of three tours (Timeline, Colonial Conquests, Geo) and choose how long and how complex the texts should be: every object has nine versions of its text for each tour, 810 in all. Each object page explains how the object left, who claims it and who holds it, with the sources for each position. An atlas traces the thirty routes on a map, and a floor plan places the objects in thirteen rooms over two floors.
projects.conclusionText: Developed for Information Modeling and Web Technologies (prof. Fabio Vitali) in the Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge master's at the University of Bologna. Built in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with inline SVG maps, 3D views of the objects, an RDF graph for every record, and dark and light themes.
projects.highlightCaption: Home page: the thirty objects, five continents, thirteen rooms, two floors and three tours.
projects.context: Information Modeling and Web Technologies (prof. Fabio Vitali), MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna
projects.reworkNote: The Stolen Archive began as a group project with Corrado Consiglio and Marco Lamorte for Information Modeling and Web Technologies. I reworked it independently in 2026; the version shown here is that rework.

summary.brief: Museums rarely show how colonial-era objects left home, who claims them and who holds them today.
summary.role: Information modeling and web development; the 2026 redesign on my own.
summary.method: A metadata model for 30 objects; 810 texts across 3 tours, 3 lengths and 3 reading levels; maps, floor plans and 3D views.
summary.outcome: A virtual exhibition of 30 objects in 13 rooms on two floors, each with the claims, holdings and sources behind it.
summary.stack: HTML · CSS · JavaScript · Leaflet · three.js · RDF

projects.shows: Information architecture for difficult, contested content, and a public interface built end to end.

projects.title: Digitalian Folktales
projects.description: A searchable digital edition that sets Calvino's Italian folktales beside the dialect versions he drew on.
projects.introText: Digitalian Folktales is a digital edition of tales from Italo Calvino's Fiabe italiane, read alongside the regional versions Calvino drew on.

gridImages.caption: Parallel reading: the Friulian field record beside its Italian translation, aligned passage by passage so each can be cited, with a map of related tales and the tale's record card.
Comparing stories: the Friulian and Sicilian cycles as catalog cards, showing the tale type (ATU 774) they share.
Search in use: 'lepre' (hare) finds episode II of the Friulian cycle, La coratella di lepre.

projects.middleText: The comparison view sets two versions of the same tale side by side, such as Gesù e San Pietro in Friuli and in Sicilia, each with its original dialect text and an Italian translation. For every tale the edition records where it comes from, its narrators, Calvino's source collection, its ATU tale type and a Propp-based reading of its outcome, animals and places, and an advanced search runs across the corpus.
projects.conclusionText: The 2026 version makes the edition usable: a search that finds tales and episodes, the dialect record beside the Italian passage by passage, a map of the tales, catalog cards comparing the two cycles, an Italian and English interface and a guide to the sources (Calvino, Zorzùt, Pitrè).
projects.highlightCaption: The search page: find a tale or an episode by keyword.
projects.context: MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna
projects.reworkNote: Digitalian Folktales began as a group project with Nikolai Gorbachev. I reworked it independently in 2026; the version shown here is that rework.

summary.brief: Calvino retold Italy's folktales in standard Italian; the dialect versions he drew on are hard to read against his.
summary.role: Edition design and web development; the 2026 rework on my own.
summary.method: Dialect texts aligned with Italian translations passage by passage; tale types (ATU) and a structural reading recorded for each episode.
summary.outcome: A searchable edition of two tale cycles, Friuli and Sicily: 5 episodes cataloged, 15 aligned passages.

projects.shows: Turning scholarly source material into something people can search and read side by side.

projects.title: Cognitive Bias Ontology
projects.description: Sixteen OWL ontologies of cognitive biases, and an explorer that walks through each user story as a graph and tests every competency question with SPARQL.
projects.introText: An ontology for a cluster of cognitive biases, part of a collective ontology of human biases built by the whole class of Knowledge Representation and Extraction (prof. Aldo Gangemi, University of Bologna, 2022/23).

gridImages.caption: The Gambler's Fallacy ontology drawn from its OWL file: the lottery user story as individuals and relations, with each class marked by where it comes from.
Story walk: the Gambler's Fallacy user story sentence by sentence; the individuals each sentence describes are outlined, the ones not yet reached are faint.

A competency question tested: the fixed query runs in the browser and its answer, the recent memory, is marked on the graph. The GitBook's own query asked for the inverse property and returned nothing.
Gambler's fallacy and the hot-hand fallacy side by side: mirror-image biases, with the classes and properties both models use marked in each.
Reuse matrix: which design patterns and Framester frames each of the 16 ontologies actually uses in its user-story graph, and which it only documents.
Filtering by design pattern: selecting Affected By picks out the seven ontologies whose user stories are built on it.

projects.middleText: Our group, Marco Lamorte, Corrado Consiglio, Salvatore Di Marzo and I, modeled sixteen biases, from the gambler's fallacy and the hot hand fallacy to pareidolia, naive realism and the blind spot bias. Each went through the same eXtreme Design workflow: research and documentation, ideation and design, modeling and implementation, then presentation and visualization. ChatGPT and Gemini were used early on for definitions, scenarios and user stories, and Framester among the resources for modeling.
projects.conclusionText: The process is documented in a public GitBook. It showed how much understanding of a domain an ontology needs before any modeling starts, and where language models help and where their answers had to be corrected. In 2026 I built an explorer on the group's OWL files: it walks through each user story sentence by sentence as the graph fills in, compares any two ontologies, and runs every competency question as SPARQL in the browser. Testing showed what the documentation did not: only 12 of the group's 24 written queries answered their question as written, mostly because of reversed properties and typos. Fixed and completed, 37 of the 47 questions are answered by the files, 7 in part, and 3 ask about things the files do not record.
projects.highlightCaption: The explorer's overview: 16 ontologies, 119 classes, 52 object properties and 121 user-story assertions.
projects.context: Knowledge Representation and Extraction (prof. Aldo Gangemi), 2022/23, MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna
projects.reworkNote: The ontologies were built as a group project with Marco Lamorte, Corrado Consiglio and Salvatore Di Marzo for Knowledge Representation and Extraction (2022/23). In 2026 I independently built a visual explorer from the group's OWL files and documentation, and tested every competency question against them; the images here come from it.

summary.brief: Cognitive biases are described in prose; there was no shared formal model to query them.
summary.role: Four of the sixteen ontologies, in a team of four; the 2026 explorer on my own.
summary.method: eXtreme Design: user stories, competency questions, ontology design patterns and alignment to Framester; in 2026, every competency question tested as SPARQL.
summary.outcome: 16 OWL ontologies (119 classes, 52 object properties) and an explorer that walks through each story and tests all 47 competency questions: 37 are answered by the files.
summary.stack: OWL · RDF · SPARQL · Python (rdflib, owlready2) · JavaScript · Oxigraph

facts: competency questions, each run as SPARQL
projects.shows: Structured knowledge modeling in a team, and testing a model against its own requirements.

projects.title: wipEU
projects.description: An open-data visualization of women in EU decision-making: every seat as a real person, how the roles line up across countries, and how the share of women falls at the top of each body.
projects.introText: wipEU is an open data project on how the representation of women in positions of power and decision-making correlates across the European Union, and how it has changed over time.

gridImages.caption: The chamber: one dot per person. In 2023, 44 of 164 leaders of major EU-27 political parties were women.
Two years at once: the dashed line marks where the women's seats ended in 2011, the shaded band the ground gained since.
The research question, answered: how closely six roles rank the EU-27 countries alike, for any year, with the scatter of the selected pair.
The higher the seat, the fewer the women: in six of eight bodies the top level has a smaller share of women than the level below.
Pace to parity: a straight-line trend through the last ten years, labeled as a projection.
Across Europe: the share of women by country on a map, with a ranked list against the EU-27 figure.
Country profiles: Italy against the EU-27 and parity across three datasets.

projects.middleText: We combined EIGE datasets across six areas (public administration, business and finance, politics, environment and climate change, education and research, law and institutions) into new mashup datasets, and assessed their quality, legal and ethical aspects as open data. In 2026 I redesigned the site around seats: a hemicycle for each body with one dot per real person, which can show a single country and the first year beside the latest. The site now answers its own question directly: rank correlations between six roles across the EU-27, for every year, with a scatter for each pair and a plain reading of how much to trust it. Alongside them sit a pace-to-parity projection, a country map and profiles.
projects.conclusionText: The answer is looser than the question hoped: in 2022 only two of twelve pairs of roles from different areas line up more than chance would give, and one role, senior civil servants in environment ministries, runs the other way. What holds almost everywhere is a ceiling: in six of eight bodies women hold a smaller share of the top seats than of the level below. Final project for Open Access and Digital Ethics (2023/24, University of Bologna) with Salvatore Di Marzo and Matteo Guenci; I worked on the idea, data retrieval, the visualizations, the quality and legal analyses and the website. The mashup datasets are released under CC BY 4.0.
projects.highlightCaption: The research question: how does the representation of women in decision-making positions correlate across the EU, and how has it changed?
projects.context: Open Access and Digital Ethics, 2023/24, MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna
projects.reworkNote: wipEU began as a group project with Salvatore Di Marzo and Matteo Guenci for Open Access and Digital Ethics (2023/24). I reworked it independently in 2026; the version shown here is that rework.

summary.brief: Data on women in EU decision-making is scattered across EIGE tables, and headcounts hide how far each body is from parity.
summary.role: Idea, data retrieval, visualization, quality and legal analysis, website; the 2026 rework on my own.
summary.method: EIGE datasets for six areas merged into mashups; shares computed from headcounts and checked against EIGE's own percentages; Spearman rank correlations across the EU-27 for every year.
summary.outcome: No area reaches parity; roles line up only loosely across countries, and in six of eight bodies the top level has fewer women than the level below.
summary.stack: D3.js · JavaScript · Python · EIGE open data

facts: policy areas merged from EIGE data

bodies with fewer women at the top
projects.shows: Open-data research with a quality, legal and ethics review, and a research question answered with the data rather than illustrated.

projects.title: The Meme Ontology
projects.description: An OWL 2 knowledge graph of 5,000 internet memes, grounded in bibliographic and iconological theory, with interactive visualizations, a SPARQL explorer and the full thesis online.
projects.introText: MEMO is an ontology of internet memes, from my master's research Towards an Ontology of Memes (supervisor Fabio Vitali), which I began as a visiting research fellow at the Institute of Network Cultures in Amsterdam, for its Viral Image Cultures project.

gridImages.caption: Temporal distribution of memes by format.
Platform of origin over time.
Memes placed by creative productivity against cultural prominence.
Variant gallery: memes grouped by the dimension along which they are transformed.
Variant family tree: one meme and its variants, with the color spectrum of the set.
SPARQL explorer with example queries over the knowledge graph.

projects.middleText: Following Lev Manovich's cultural analytics, it treats memes as a large dataset rather than isolated texts. Around 5,000 images and their metadata, scraped from Know Your Meme, are described in an OWL ontology informed by FRBR across three areas: visual content, cultural references and format. CLIP is used to classify them semi-automatically.
projects.conclusionText: The ontology is published with LODE documentation, interactive visualizations of formats, platforms, periods and variants, and a SPARQL explorer with example queries, including links to Wikidata for regions and platforms.
projects.highlightCaption: Home page: the project title above a wall of memes from the Know Your Meme sample, which can be rearranged by year, colour or format. Hovering a tile shows its RDF.
projects.context: Master's thesis (supervisor Fabio Vitali), MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna; begun as a visiting research fellowship at the Institute of Network Cultures (Viral Image Cultures)

summary.brief: A large, messy cultural dataset with no structured model to classify, link or query it.
summary.role: Sole researcher: data collection, ontology, classification and visualization.
summary.method: About 5,000 Know Your Meme entries scraped; an OWL ontology informed by FRBR; CLIP for semi-automatic classification.
summary.outcome: A published ontology (206,923 triples) with documentation, eleven interactive visualizations, a SPARQL explorer linked to Wikidata and the full thesis as an indexed reader.
summary.stack: Python · CLIP · OWL 2 / Protégé · SPARQL (Comunica) · D3.js

facts: memes scraped from Know Your Meme
RDF triples in the populated ontology
projects.shows: Data modeling and knowledge-graph construction at scale: scraping, ontology design, semi-automatic classification and a queryable SPARQL endpoint.

overview.label: Role
overview.value: Sole researcher: data collection, ontology design, classification, visualization and web development

overview.label: Context
overview.value: Master's thesis, MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna (supervisor Fabio Vitali; co-supervisors Tommaso Campagna, Carlo Teo Pedretti); begun as a visiting research fellowship at the Institute of Network Cultures, Amsterdam

overview.label: Methods
overview.value: Web scraping, purposive sampling, ontology engineering (FRBR/LRM, Panofsky), CLIP zero-shot classification, manual annotation, cultural analytics

overview.label: Tools
overview.value: Python, CLIP ViT-B/32, EasyOCR, rdflib, Protégé, Comunica, D3.js, Netlify

context.text: Internet memes are one of the largest and least formally organized bodies of visual culture of the twenty-first century. Know Your Meme documents them in depth, but as a community wiki: there was no formal, theory-grounded model to classify meme templates, their visual properties and the way their variants transform them. MEMO (the MEMe Ontology) is that model, built and tested on a corpus of 5,000 entries.

goals.title: A formal model
goals.text: Extend bibliographic (FRBR/LRM) and iconological (Panofsky) frameworks so memes can be classified without flattening their cultural complexity.

goals.title: Culture at corpus scale
goals.text: Make structural patterns in meme culture (formats, platforms, periods, variants) visible and queryable, following Manovich’s cultural analytics.

items.title: Ontological
items.text: Which formal framework can classify memes as cultural and digital objects, and how must FRBR and Panofsky’s iconological method be extended to fit them?

items.title: Computational
items.text: How far can CLIP zero-shot classification describe the pre-iconographical level of 5,000 meme images, and where does it fail?

items.title: Cultural analytics
items.text: Which temporal, relational and platform patterns become visible only when memes are analysed as a corpus?

items.title: Archival
items.text: How can a community archive like Know Your Meme become a machine-readable research corpus while keeping the integrity of its folksonomy metadata?

sections.title: Pipeline
sections.lead: Four stages, each producing the structured input for the next, adapted from Manovich’s operations for cultural analytics.

items.title: Three datasets
items.text: A random sample of 5,000 Know Your Meme entries with images and metadata; D0, a purposive subset of 50; and 391 variant images from the galleries of 43 D0 entries.

items.title: Two axes of classification
items.text: An OWL 2 DL ontology built in Protégé along FRBR/LRM levels (MemeIdea, MemeConcept, VariantInstance) and Panofsky’s levels of meaning, reusing Wikidata, schema.org and Dublin Core.

items.title: CLIP and manual annotation
items.text: CLIP ViT-B/32 zero-shot labels for image type, subject, text and colour on all 5,000 images; hand annotation of cultural references and of how 50 variants transform their template.

items.title: A public web platform
items.text: D3.js visualizations of the whole corpus, D0 and the variants, alongside the ontology documentation, an in-browser SPARQL endpoint and the thesis text.

sections.title: The ontology
sections.lead: 33 classes, 28 object properties and 14 data properties. The main contribution is a transformation typology at the Expression level (TransformationDimension and TransformationExtent), which neither FRBR nor iconography provides: it records how, and how far, a variant departs from its template.

items.alt: Interactive graph of MEMO classes: MemeConcept, VariantInstance, MemeFormat and CulturalReference with their subclasses and properties
items.caption: The ontology as an interactive graph: MEMO classes in black, reused FRBR, schema.org and Wikidata classes dashed.

items.alt: SPARQL explorer with a query for the most viewed Exploitable memes and a results table
items.caption: SPARQL explorer: the 206,923 triples are queried in the browser with Comunica, with example queries and deep links.

items.alt: Dataset page with three cards for the global dataset, the D0 sample and the variants
items.caption: The three datasets, each browsable and filterable by format and platform.

sections.title: Corpus visualizations
sections.lead: The first three views read the whole corpus: when formats appear, which ones draw attention and how platforms succeed each other.

items.alt: Bubble matrix of meme formats by year
items.caption: Temporal distribution of format: Exploitable, ImageMacro and Catchphrase run through every period, while TikTok-native formats cluster after 2021.

items.alt: Bubble chart of average views per meme format
items.caption: Popularity × format: Reaction and ViralVideo draw more views than their share of the corpus.

items.alt: Stacked bars of origin platform by period
items.caption: Platform × period: from YouTube and Twitter before 2010 to the rise of TikTok after 2021.

items.alt: Streamgraph of meme origin platforms from 2004 to 2025 with a chapter card
items.caption: Platform story: a scroll-driven streamgraph whose chapters are computed from the data.

items.alt: Sankey diagram from origin platform to format, image type and text presence
items.caption: Property flow: every meme traced from platform to format, image type and text.

sections.title: Variants and transformation
sections.lead: The D0 sample and its variants show what the ontology’s Expression level adds: a meme’s views and its creative productivity are separate things. Karen has over 13,000 documented variants at 2 million views; Me Gusta has hundreds at 9 million.

items.alt: Scatter plot of the 50 D0 memes by views and number of variants
items.caption: Creative productivity × cultural prominence for the 50 D0 memes, drawn as their images.

items.alt: Rows of variant thumbnails sorted from minimal to parody
items.caption: Variant gallery: 50 annotated variants of five templates, from minimal change to parody.

items.alt: Radial tree with the original meme at the centre and its variants on rings by transformation extent
items.caption: Variant family tree: rings are transformation extent, sectors the main dimension; hovering a variant swaps it into the centre.

sections.title: Exploring the graph
sections.lead: Three views make the knowledge graph and the classifier tangible, rather than only summarising them.

items.alt: Force graph of memes and property chips expanding from one meme
items.caption: Knowledge-graph walk: a meme opens into its properties and a property pulls in other memes that share it; each node links to a SPARQL query.

items.alt: Every meme drawn as a coloured dot on a colour wheel
items.caption: Colour spectrum: all 5,000 memes as their average colour, rearranged by year, hue or lightness.

items.alt: Dot plot of CLIP confidence per image type with a threshold line
items.caption: Classifier confidence: at a 0.80 threshold, 61.7% of CLIP labels would not survive.

sections.title: The thesis, online
sections.lead: The dissertation is published on the site as an indexed reader, generated from the final PDF: 61 headings, full-text search with section context, figures, a linked bibliography and page numbers that match the printed edition.

items.alt: Thesis reader with a sticky index and the abstract
items.caption: Thesis reader with its index, reading progress and a title strip of memes from the corpus.

items.alt: Thesis reader showing search results for Panofsky
items.caption: Full-text search: results grouped by section, and each hit highlighted in the text.

sections.title: Visual identity
sections.lead: The site had to read as a thesis and as a meme archive at once. Titles use Impact, the typeface of the meme caption; the rest is quiet ink on paper, so the memes are the only colour. Memes from the corpus are used as graphic material: in title strips, on the home wall and in a random-meme card available on every page.

items.alt: Home page on a phone
items.caption: Home

items.alt: Random meme card on a phone
items.caption: Random meme

items.alt: Variant family tree on a phone
items.caption: Variant family tree

items.alt: Thesis reader on a phone
items.caption: Thesis reader

items.title: FRBR, extended, fits memes
items.text: Idea, template and variant are distinct entities that carry different information, and the transformation typology adds what neither FRBR nor iconography models.

items.title: CLIP helps, but cannot be trusted alone
items.text: Image-type labels are plausible (Cartoon 45.3%, Photograph 44.8%), but zero-shot classification always picks a label; 34.4% of subjects fell back to Unknown and the rest lack ground truth.

items.title: Patterns only visible at scale
items.text: Durable foundational formats, the move from static images to short-form video, and format as a predictor of reach.

items.title: Folksonomy as evidence
items.text: Using Wikidata’s publisher property for platform keeps community attributions as assertions rather than claims of objective provenance.

reflection: The ontology works best where it is most theoretical: separating the template from its variants is what made the decoupling of views and variants visible at all.

The weakest layer is the automatic one. Next time I would run several classification passes with different prompts and keep only the labels they agree on, flagging the rest for review: fewer assertions, but ones the analysis can rely on.
Publishing the thesis, the data and the queries together turned a written argument into something people can check and explore themselves.

projects.title: Culture4All
projects.description: A data story on unequal access to culture in Italy, from ISTAT and Ministry of Culture open data: follow your region through every chart, from libraries and distance to reading over ten years.
projects.introText: Culture for All maps access to culture across Italy: where libraries, archives and museums are, how far people live from a library, how libraries are used, and how reading habits differ and change from region to region.

gridImages.caption: Counting libraries rewards big provinces; per inhabitant, the map changes.
Where the cultural institutions are, next to the share of municipalities with no library, by region.
Southern libraries lend a fraction of what northern ones do: loans per public library, 2022.
Where libraries lend less, fewer people read: reading habits by region, 2021.
Follow a region: pick one and it stays highlighted in every chart, with a profile of where it stands on seven measures, a link and a shareable image.
How far is the nearest library? 3.5 million people live in a municipality without one, but for half of those municipalities one is within 3.9 km.
Reading from 2011 to 2021: the north–south gap narrowed because the north read less, not because the south read more.
The findings, each linked back to its chart, and how every number was made.

projects.middleText: Built on open data from ISTAT and the Ministry of Culture, the 2026 version is a data story on unequal access to culture. It sets ISTAT's rate of libraries per 10,000 inhabitants beside the raw counts, measures the straight-line distance from every municipality without a library to the nearest one, and follows reading habits from 2011 to 2021. Readers can follow one region through every chart. Each chart states its finding, explains how to read it in plain language and has a data table behind it.
projects.conclusionText: Distance is rarely the barrier: the widest gap is in how libraries are used, with southern libraries lending a fraction of what northern ones do, and reading is falling everywhere but Umbria. The data also has blind spots: regions that run their own heritage, like Sicily, almost vanish from the Ministry's events data. Made for Information Visualization (2023/24, University of Bologna) with Corrado Consiglio and Salvatore Di Marzo, who gathered and cleaned the data; I designed the visualizations and built the site, and reworked it on my own in 2026 with D3.js and Python. A comprehension test plan for the charts is published in the repository.

projects.title: Unobravo Redesign
projects.description: A research-led redesign of Unobravo's website and app that makes starting online therapy easier to understand, compare and trust.
projects.introText: Unobravo connects people with therapists over video call. Its website tried to be a marketing page, a guide and an onboarding flow at once, and the app offered no explanation of the service at all. I redesigned both, from interviews to a tested Figma prototype.
projects.middleText: The research combined interviews across three age groups, a competitor study of Serenis, expert reviews and think-aloud testing. It surfaced nine usability issues: an overwhelming "how it works" page, calls to action that pushed people into the questionnaire before they understood the service, opaque therapist matching, scheduling that ignored stated preferences, a full test to repeat just to change therapist, no way to compare profiles, hidden pricing and privacy information, and an app whose navigation was buried in a sidebar.
projects.conclusionText: Over three iterations the design added a calmer home page, a real dashboard with the next appointment and pricing, three therapist proposals with a "why you match" explanation, filters to compare profiles, and a way to change therapist by only updating preferences. In the summative test of the final version, all four participants completed every task with no errors, and the average SUS score rose from 75 on the original product to 91.25.

context.text: Unobravo is a leading European online psychology service, founded in Italy in 2019, that matches people with licensed therapists over video call. Many potential users hesitate: they worry about privacy, doubt that online therapy can feel human, and don't understand how the matching works. The goal was to reduce that reluctance and make the service easy to understand and trust, across ages and levels of digital literacy.

goals.title: Transparency
goals.text: Explain data practices, pricing and the matching process clearly, so privacy concerns can be resolved rather than hidden in a footer.

goals.title: Personalization
goals.text: Adapt the journey to different needs and levels of readiness, from someone just exploring to someone ready to book.

methods.title: Segmentation
methods.text: Three age groups (25–34, 35–44, 45–55) crossed with the Stages of Change model. The focus segment: young adults in the Preparation stage.

methods.title: Interviews and market research
methods.text: Four young adults, two mid-career and two mature adults, plus published data on Gen Z mental health, stigma and access to support.

methods.title: Expert review
methods.text: Direct and reverse checkpoint reviews of Unobravo and its competitor Serenis, on website and app.

methods.title: Preliminary testing
methods.text: Four tasks on each product: understand the service, take the matching test, change therapist, compare profiles. SUS on the original: 75.

methods.title: Service blueprint and information architecture
methods.text: Mapped the current and proposed journeys for the website and app, then restructured the IA to separate explanation from conversion.

methods.title: Personas
methods.text: A protagonist persona and a supporting cast of six, used to test decisions against different ages, needs and attitudes to therapy.

persona.name: Luca Taglioni
persona.facts: 29 · graphic designer in Milan · high digital proficiency · anxiety, panic attacks, sleep difficulties
persona.quote: There is hope, even when your brain tells you there isn't.
persona.story: Friends in therapy have encouraged Luca to start, and he feels ready. He expects polished, personal digital products and dislikes rigid, bureaucratic flows. He will invest time and money, but only if the platform feels trustworthy and human.
needs: A clean, professional interface that still feels warm, not clinical
Filters and recommendations tailored to anxiety and sleep issues
A frictionless booking flow with availability, cost and policies up front
Reassuring, empathetic microcopy for a first-time therapy user

issues.title: Overwhelming and unclear “How it works” experience
issues.evidence: No tested user could explain how Unobravo works. “Oh my god, there is so much stuff here.”

issues.title: Calls to action push people into the questionnaire too early
issues.evidence: Users clicked “Trova il tuo Unobravo” expecting an explanation, and landed in the test.

issues.title: Matching logic is opaque
issues.evidence: The promised three profiles were not delivered, and users were forced to retake the test.

issues.title: Scheduling ignores stated preferences
issues.evidence: A morning preference was ignored, with no explanation when slots were unavailable.

issues.title: Changing therapist means retaking the whole test
issues.evidence: Users repeated the full questionnaire just to change availability.

issues.title: No way to compare therapists
issues.evidence: The “compare profiles” task failed for every user; the index was missing from the app.

issues.title: Pricing and privacy are hard to find
issues.evidence: Users searched the wrong sections and misremembered prices; privacy lived only in the footer.

issues.title: Weak navigation and no escape routes
issues.evidence: Back options and orientation cues were missing along key flows.

issues.title: App navigation hidden in a sidebar
issues.evidence: The app offered no explanation of the service and no dashboard for ongoing therapy.

recommendations.title: Separate explaining from converting
recommendations.text: A non-transactional “Scopri Unobravo” path explains the service, matching, costs and privacy before anyone is asked to start the test.

recommendations.title: Calmer calls to action
recommendations.text: “Scopri come funziona” sits next to “Inizia”, so users choose between exploring and committing.

recommendations.title: Make matching explicit
recommendations.text: Always three proposals, each with a “Why we chose this therapist for you” explanation.

recommendations.title: Decouple preferences from matching
recommendations.text: Change schedule or preferences without retaking the full questionnaire.

iterations.text: First restructuring: an explanatory entry point, a pill-shaped tab bar instead of the sidebar, a dashboard.

iterations.name: Version 1
iterations.text: Added change and delete appointment, clearer therapy progress, and routes to the therapist profile.

iterations.name: Version 2 · final
iterations.text: Three proposals with match explanations, filters to compare profiles, change therapist from the first screen, quick actions.

flows.caption: 01 · Onboarding and discovery: from first contact to an informed choice of path
02 · Matching questionnaire: one question at a time, visible progress, support always at hand
03 · Professionals portal: browse, filter and compare profiles independently
04 · Proposals and booking: three explained proposals, booking in two taps, clear payment
05 · Personal area: next appointment, chat, invoices and diary in one tab bar
06 · Online session: from device check to feedback without leaving the app

Booking confirmed: the success mark settles with a soft overshoot
Video session: controls slide in and the live indicator pulses

prototype.text: The full prototype is wired in Figma as one continuous prototype, from first visit to the video session: about 240 connections across six flows, with interactive answer options, filter sheets and smart-animated questionnaire progress. Try it below, or open it in Figma.

system.text: Behind the screens is a small design system: 34 variables (10 primitives, 13 semantic colors, 7 spacing and 4 radius values), 14 text styles, 31 components and 33 icons. Every text color passes WCAG AA contrast and every touch target is at least 44 px.

images.caption: Cards: option, price, therapist, appointment, calendar
Illustrations for sections, success and support

results.text: Four participants completed every task on the final version, working alone while recording their screen, with no errors. Scores also became more consistent as the design matured (variance fell from 58.33 to 29.69). Participants singled out the “why this therapist” explanation as what made the matching feel trustworthy.

reflection: The biggest change was structural, not visual: separating “understand the service” from “start the test” fixed three critical issues at once. For a mental-health service, trust comes from transparency: showing how matching works, what it costs and what happens to your data.

The final version adds what a real product would need next: crisis support and health-data consent in the questionnaire, empty and error states, and the online session itself. The samples were small (three to four people per round), so the next step would be a larger test across all age segments.

projects.title: Words of Gender
projects.description: A digital archive of women authors that follows how writers across five centuries wrote about the same gendered concepts.
projects.introText: Words of Gender is the prototype of an archive of women authors. Taking its lead from Vera Gheno's Parole d'altro genere (Rizzoli, 2023), it asks how different authors, in different historical and cultural contexts, have written about the same concepts tied to gender: beauty, grace, strength, independence, marriage, maternity.
projects.middleText: Excerpts from nine women authors spanning five centuries (1558 to 1958), in Italian, French and English, are encoded in TEI XML and linked to VIAF, Wikidata and WorldCat. 172 passages are tagged with 27 concepts, so each concept can be followed across texts as a network of variations and cross-references rather than read one author at a time.
projects.conclusionText: The 2026 version turns the prototype into a reading edition: a reading view where up to four concepts are highlighted at once, never by color alone; an author-by-concept matrix that opens every passage on a concept side by side; and a timeline of first editions.

resume.description: I'm an HCI researcher and designer based in Amsterdam. I start from how people actually use technology, test ideas with them, and turn what I learn into clear, inclusive interfaces, data visualizations and working prototypes. My background is in cultural anthropology and digital humanities; I'm now doing an MSc in Human-Computer Interaction at the University of Amsterdam.

about.lead: Research comes first: I start from how people actually use technology, test ideas with them, and turn what I learn into clear, inclusive interfaces, data visualizations and working prototypes.
paragraphs: My background is in cultural anthropology and digital humanities, so research comes first: interviews, usability tests, fieldwork and data analysis. From there I design and build, in Figma and in code.

I've worked as a UX researcher and designer at BrainBite, an AI tutoring platform for children, on support for neurodiverse learners; done practice-based research as a visiting research fellow at the Institute of Network Cultures; and taken part in The Hmm's Voices of Makers program with DEN. My projects deal with museum collections, archives, public data and online therapy, and I care that the result is inclusive, well evidenced and easy to use.
